families.s: HSE rubber-ingredient bag-opening and weighing control guidance
families.t: powder ingredients, bag opening, weighing, dust extraction, containment, cleaning, waste, PPE and exposure measurement
f: Rubber COSHH guidance provides a specific control sheet for bag opening and weighing ingredients.
The task can generate rubber process dust before ingredients are incorporated into uncured elastomer.
Dust extraction should capture releases at the opening and weighing point.
Containers and transfer methods should minimise pouring height and spillage.
Cleaning should avoid redistributing fine dust.
Waste bags and contaminated material should be contained.
RPE may be required for residual exposure or exceptional tasks.
Exposure measurement and health surveillance should be considered where risk remains.
families.g: Bag-opening and weighing risk depends on ingredient hazard and dustiness, bag and transfer method, quantity, enclosure and extraction, cleaning, waste handling, PPE and exposure duration.

families.s: HSE rubber mixing and two-roll milling dust-and-fume control guidance
families.t: ingredient mixing, two-roll mills, dust, fume, local extraction, nip hazards, access, temperature, maintenance and safe intervention
f: Rubber COSHH sheets address ingredient mixing and milling on two-roll mills.
Mixing can release dust from ingredients and additives.
Milling can release both dust and fume.
Local extraction should be positioned to capture emissions without creating unsafe access.
Rotating rolls create severe in-running nip hazards.
Cleaning, adjustment and blockage clearing need safe intervention arrangements.
Temperature and compound condition influence fume generation.
Guards, trips, isolation and extraction should be inspected and maintained together.
families.g: Mixing and milling risk depends on ingredients, process temperature, roll speed and nip access, dust and fume generation, extraction, guards and trips, intervention, isolation and maintenance.

families.s: HSE rubber-press and curing-fume control guidance
families.t: rubber presses, moulding, curing ovens, hot compounds, fume extraction, press movement, guarding, unloading, maintenance and exposure control
f: Rubber COSHH guidance includes control sheets for rubber presses and curing-related fume.
Curing ovens and hot moulding processes can release rubber fume.
General or local ventilation should control fume near curing and pressing operations.
Press closing and opening movement creates crushing hazards.
Guards and interlocks should prevent access during dangerous movement.
Loading and unloading methods should reduce contact with hot moulds and compounds.
Cleaning and maintenance require isolation of electrical, hydraulic and pneumatic energy.
Process and exposure controls should be checked after compound, temperature or cycle changes.
families.g: Press and curing risk depends on compound and temperature, fume release, press movement and force, guarding and interlocks, loading and unloading, heat, isolation, ventilation and maintenance.

families.s: HSE rubber-machinery safe-intervention and unexpected-start prevention guidance
families.t: blockage clearing, adjustment, planned maintenance, separation, perimeter fencing, close guarding, safe electrical isolation, failure modes and permits
f: Many rubber-industry injuries occur during adjustment, blockage clearing or maintenance interventions.
Unplanned malfunction interventions are less predictable than planned maintenance.
Dangerous moving parts and people should remain separated until equipment is safe.
Safeguarding may use interlocked perimeter fencing or close guarding of individual machines.
Safe electrical isolation should normally be the first option in the control hierarchy.
Isolation must include precautions against inadvertent reconnection.
Assessment should identify access frequency, failure modes, adjacent danger zones and who controls the risk.
Special maintenance arrangements may require permits, lock-off and controlled test or setup modes.
families.g: Safe-intervention risk depends on failure mode and urgency, access and visibility, energy sources and stored energy, safeguarding architecture, isolation and lock-off, number of people, permits and competence.

families.s: HSE machinery locking-device and trapped-key guidance for rubber processing
families.t: padlocks, trapped keys, lockable covers, isolators, multiple people, whole-body access, restart prevention, gate closure and maintenance
f: Machinery locking devices can include padlock facilities, trapped-key interlocks and lockable covers or enclosures.
The number of keys required depends on the machine and the number of people needing protection.
A separate isolation point can allow the person entering to lock off the energy supply.
Where a gate could be closed with someone inside and out of sight, additional key control may be required.
The person in the danger area should remain in control of restart prevention.
Whole-body access requires controls against inadvertent restart after a gate is closed.
Maintenance normally requires the machine isolator to be locked off.
Locking-device arrangements should be tested, documented and included in training and supervision.
families.g: Locking-device risk control depends on machine and access layout, energy isolation, number and visibility of people, key logic, whole-body entry, restart paths, maintenance task and supervision.
